The result was that the mill levy decreased from 44.89 mills in 1972 to 24.00 mills in 1976 (See Table III-9). In the high school district, expenditures and taxable valuation increased by similar magnitudes, and the proportion of district financed expenditures was cut in half. The resulting decrease in mill levy was slight, from 14.50 mills in 1972 to 12.39 mills in 1976.
Revenue Overview, 1976 - Big Horn County has had major increases in taxable value in recent years, primarily as a result of coal mining, and revenues have increased considerably. In addition, the county automatically receives four percent of the Montana Coal Severance Tax receipts from levies on coal within the county. In F.Y. 1977, this is projected to amount to $2,674,625 (Hardin Herald, November 13, 1975, p. 1). At the same time, there has been little increase in demand on county services and little is expected (see previous section). As a result, the county has been able to lower the mill levy and maintain current service levels. The Big Horn County Clerk does not see any budget strains for the county government in the near future (Joyce Lippert, Big Horn County Clerk, personal interview, January 8, 1976).
Again, Hardin and Lodge Grass face strikingly different situations relative to the county. Mill levies in both towns have reached the constitutional limit of 65.00 mills (with special funds up to 2.5 mills) and both are beginning to operate in the red. Any increase in revenue must come from increases in taxable valuation.
